newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds drift off with declining U.S. T-bonds.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds drift off with declining U.S. T-bonds.

text.p: Irish bonds drifted off after a firm start on Tuesday in sympathy with declining U.S. Treasuries, dealers said.

"Treasuries have been quite a bit weaker since the U.S. market opened today and have continually drifted," a dealer said. "Central banks have been selling at the short end and hedge funds are selling 10-year futures contracts, pushing the long end down."

U.S. Treasuries drifted sideways in quiet trade in London as the market dithered over direction ahead of a stream of data releases later in the week, including the U.S. Federal Reserve's economic outlook, the Beige Book, due on Wednesday.
Earlier, five-year and 10-year Irish bonds had been up 10 pence and 20 pence respectively, following a curve-flattening trend in Europe, dealers said.

"Curve flattening was the dominant theme across Europe yesterday and that's been affecting the Irish market," a dealer said. "But this has been offset by the prospect of supply in the 10-year bond expected next week."

Dealers said that activity would be capped by supply factors ahead of next Tuesday's auction by Ireland's National Treasury Management Agency of 150 million Irish pounds of the eight percent bond due 2006.
Otherwise, with weak growth and low inflation in Europe, dealers said, the backdrop in Europe was encouraging.

"The view is that German interest rates are unlikely to drop - and may even go higher - and this coupled with a lack of inflation threat is generally supportive of long yields," a dealer said. "Thus we're seeing long yields trending down."

By 1600 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down seven pence from Monday's close to 101.95 to yield 5.99 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 fell five pence from the close to 109.55 to yield 6.60 percent.
